article.title: How to close your books in five working days
article.excerpt: A routine for small businesses that turns month-end from a chore into numbers you can act on.

author.name: Ana Ruiz
author.bio: Ana has closed the books for more than two hundred small businesses. She writes about the routines that make month-end boring, in the best way.

heroImage.alt: Printed invoices and a calculator on a desk

content.html:
Most small businesses close their books three or four weeks after the month ends. By then the numbers are history: useful for tax, but too late to change anything. A five-day close is achievable for almost any business with fewer than fifty people, and it does not need new software. It needs a routine, a calendar and a short list of decisions you make once instead of every month.

This guide walks through the routine we use with our own clients, day by day. Each step is small. The trick is doing them in order and not letting one stuck item hold up the rest.

Why five days is the right target

Five working days is long enough to wait for bank statements, card statements and the last supplier invoices to arrive, and short enough that the month is still fresh in everyone’s mind. If you close in five days, you can look at last month’s numbers in the first week of this month, while you can still act on them: chase a late payer, pause a subscription or move a hire.

Longer closes are rarely about the volume of work. They are about waiting. Somebody waits for a receipt, somebody else waits for an answer, and the reconciliation sits half-finished. The routine below is designed to remove waiting.

Before you start: three decisions to make once

Make these decisions once, write them down and stop revisiting them every month.

Who owns the close

One person is responsible for the close finishing on day five, even if several people do parts of it. In a small business that is usually the owner or an office manager, with an external bookkeeper doing the reconciliation. Without one owner, every unanswered question is somebody else’s problem.

What “good enough” means

Decide a materiality threshold: the amount below which an unexplained difference goes on a list instead of blocking the close. For most small businesses, fifty dollars is sensible. You will still investigate those items, just not on the critical path.

Where documents live

Pick one place for receipts and invoices: a shared inbox, a folder or your accounting software’s capture address. Everybody forwards there, always. A receipt in somebody’s jacket pocket is the single most common reason a close slips.

Day 1: Reconcile bank and card accounts

Reconcile every bank and card account to its statement balance on the last day of the month. Bank feeds make this mostly a matter of confirming suggested matches. Anything you cannot explain in two minutes goes on the questions list rather than blocking the reconciliation.

  • Confirm that every account has a working bank feed and that no feed stopped mid-month.
  • Match transactions to receipts; create rules for the payments that repeat every month.
  • Record transfers between your own accounts as transfers, not as income and expenses.

At the end of day one, every account should show a zero difference between the statement and your books, apart from items on the questions list.

Day 2: Receivables and payables

Export the aged receivables report and send reminders for anything more than thirty days overdue. It is far easier to collect an invoice that is five weeks old than one that is five months old, and a short, polite reminder at month-end becomes routine for your customers too.

Then turn to the other side: make sure every supplier invoice dated in the month is entered, even if you will pay it next month. This is what makes your profit figure honest. A month with a large unentered bill looks better than it was, and the next month looks worse.

  1. Export the aged receivables report.
  2. Send reminders for overdue invoices.
  3. Enter outstanding supplier bills and match them to purchase orders.

Day 3: Payroll, accruals and prepayments

Check that payroll journals match the payroll reports, including employer taxes and benefits. Then record accruals for costs you incurred but have not been billed for yet, such as utilities or a contractor who invoices late, and spread prepayments like annual insurance across the months they cover.

Accruals are where most small-business books are weakest, and they are what turns a bank statement into a real profit and loss account. Keep a simple accruals schedule and reverse each entry when the real invoice arrives.

The goal of a monthly close is not perfect books. It is books good enough to make a decision on.

Day 4: Review the numbers

Compare this month with last month and with the same month last year. Look for anything that moved by more than ten percent and write one sentence explaining why. Usually the explanation is mundane, such as a quarterly bill or a seasonal spike, but every so often it is a duplicate payment, a missed invoice or a cost that quietly doubled.

Work through the questions list from day one. Most items will have answers by now. The ones that do not are the ones to escalate to the owner of the close.

Day 5: Report and lock the period

Send a one-page summary to whoever runs the business: revenue, gross margin, the three biggest costs, cash in the bank and anything unusual. Then lock the period in your accounting software so nobody changes it by accident. If something needs fixing later, record an adjustment in the current month instead of reopening a closed one.

Measuring whether it is working

Track two numbers every month: the working day on which the close finished, and the number of items still on the questions list at the end of day four. The first tells you whether the routine is holding; the second tells you where it leaks. If the questions list keeps growing, the problem is almost never effort. It is usually one recurring source, such as a card that nobody reconciles, a supplier who sends invoices by post, or a manager who approves expenses in batches at the end of the quarter.

Share both numbers with whoever runs the business. A close that finishes on day five, with fewer than five open questions, is a close the business can rely on. A close that drifts to day nine is an early warning, and it is much cheaper to fix in March than in December, when the year-end deadline adds pressure to every decision you make.

Finally, review the routine itself twice a year. Remove any step that no longer catches anything, and add one for whatever surprised you most in the last six months.

Common reasons the close slips

When a client’s close starts taking longer, the cause is almost always one of these: a bank feed that silently stopped, receipts that live in several places, a supplier who invoices late every month, or a reconciliation that waits for one unanswered question. Each has a simple fix, and the fix is nearly always to decide something once rather than handling it again every month.

Start with one month. Run the routine, note where you got stuck and adjust the calendar. By the third month, the close will feel ordinary, which is exactly the point. Read our guide to accruals next, or talk to us about doing the close for you.
